newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav business community protest at high taxes.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav business community protest at high taxes.

text.p: Several hundred private businessmen demonstrated in Belgrade on Wednesday demanding tax cuts and equal treatment with state-run companies.
"The fiscal burden should correspond to the economic strength of the taxpayers," said Dragan Nikolic, president of Serbia's association of private entrepreneurs.
"But it must also correspond to the purchasing power of our consumers," he told Reuters. "The state has set exorbitant taxes and it is well known what state our economy is in."
Nikolic, who manages a firm with 275 employees, said private businessmen need consistent tax laws for at least 10 years.
"We need stable, clear and simple tax regulations which would be equally applied both to private and state-run businesses," he said.

The entrepreneurs, who gathered in a city park, demanded an end to high taxation, default payments and seizure of assets, and called on the government to revoke a law obliging every private firm and shop-keeper to employ at least two workers.
"I predict that at least 100,000 small private businesses will be closed because of this regulation," Nikolic said.
He said about 440,000 private businesses in Serbia helped the country to survive four years of crippling U.N. sanctions.
Businessmen set a November 8 deadline for the government to meet their demands. "If not, we will stage a general strike of all private entrpreneurs on November 15," Nikolic said.
The entrepreneurs' protest coincided with a wave of strikes and threatened strikes before federal and local elections set for Sunday in the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.
The authorities accuse the opposition of encouraging the strikes to stoke unrest before the polls.
Belgrade lawyers, angry at high taxes, launched a three-day protest last Monday aimed at blocking the courts.
"Wednesday is the last day of our token strike," Radmilo Milunovic of the Belgrade Bar Association said. "If our demands are not met, Belgrade lawyers will freeze their status in the association."
Such a move would amount to a permanent strike and could cause serious problems for the country's courts.
Belgrade bus and tram drivers demanding unpaid wages went on strike on Monday, stranding thousands of commuters.
Belgrade Socialist authorities broke the strike on its second day, sending in police to clear a blockade of bus garages and arresting the head of the drivers' trade union.
The mayor of Belgrade, Nebojsa Covic told state television that the drivers had been given a 10 percent raise.

Government authorities ultimately bowed to demands by striking workers in several cases over the past month, paying out overdue wages to some factory employees and adjusting tax rates for taxi drivers.
